ety.text: From Middle English knight, knyght, kniht, from Old English cniht (“boy; servant, knight”), from Proto-West Germanic *kneht.
From Middle English knighten, kniȝten, from the noun. Cognate with Middle High German knehten.

senses.d: A young servant or follower; a trained military attendant in service of a lord.
A minor nobleman with an honourable military rank who had served as a page and squire.
An armored and mounted warrior of the Middle Ages.
ex: King Arthur and the Knights of the Round Table

senses.d: A person obliged to provide knight service in exchange for maintenance of an estate held in knight's fee.
A person on whom a knighthood has been conferred by a monarch.
A brave, chivalrous and honorable man devoted to a noble cause or love interest.
A chess piece, often in the shape of a horse's head, that is moved two squares in one direction and one at right angles to that direction in a single move, leaping over any intervening pieces.
A playing card bearing the figure of a knight; the knave or jack.
Any of various nymphalid butterflies of the genus Ypthima.
Any mushroom belonging to genus Tricholoma.
To confer knighthood upon.
ex: The king knighted the young squire.

senses.d: To promote (a pawn) to a knight.

grp.label: warrior, especially of the Middle Ages
person on whom a knighthood has been conferred

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French chevalier, from Old French chevalier, from Late Latin caballārius, from Latin caballus. Doublet of cavalier.
Borrowed from Old Occitan cavalier (cf. also Old French chevalier), from Late Latin caballārius. See cavallo + -iere. Doublet of cavallaio.
From Old Spanish cavallero, inherited from Late Latin caballārius, from Latin caballus. Equivalent to caballo + -ero. Cognate with English cavalier.

pt:cavaleiro.gl: knight (heavily armoured warrior of the Middle Ages)

ety.text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cavaleiro, from Late Latin caballārius, from Latin caballus (“horse”) + -ārius. By surface analysis, cavalo (“horse”) + -eiro. Doublet of cavalheiro, through Spanish caballero.
Borrowed from Italian cavaliere, itself borrowed from Old Occitan cavalier, from Late Latin caballārius. Doublet of chevalier, which was inherited.

From Late Latin caballus (“horse”), from Latin caballus (“pack horse”), of disputed origin. Compare Portuguese cavalo, Asturian caballu, Galician cabalo, Dalmatian caval, Catalan cavall, French cheval, Spanish caballo, Romanian cal, Corsican cavallu, Sardinian cabaddu, Sicilian cavaḍḍu.
Inherited from Late Latin caballum (“horse”), from Latin caballum (“pack horse”), of disputed origin. Compare Portuguese cavalo.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cavalo, from Late Latin caballus (“horse”), from Latin caballus (“pack horse”), from Gaulish *kaballos, from Proto-Celtic *kaballos, perhaps ultimately an Asiatic borrowing or Wanderwort, compare Ancient Greek καβάλλης (kabállēs, “nag”), Proto-Slavic *kobýla (“mare”), Persian کول…
From caballo.

Inherited from Middle English knytten, from Old English cnyttan, from Proto-West Germanic *knuttijan, from Proto-Germanic *knuttijaną, from *knuttô + *-janą. Cognate with Low German knütten and Old Norse knýta (whence Danish knytte, Norwegian Nynorsk knyta). More at knot.

senses.d: To turn thread or yarn into a piece of fabric by forming loops that are pulled through each other. This can be done by hand with needles or by machine.
ex: The first generation knitted to order; the second still knits for its own use; the next leaves knitting to industrial manufacturers.

senses.d: To create a stitch by pulling the working yarn through an existing stitch from back to front.
ex: Stitches that are knitted look like little V’s when seen from the front.

senses.d: To join closely and firmly together.
ex: The fight for survival knitted the men closely together.

Lord of my love, to whom in vassalage
Thy merit hath my duty strongly knit,
To thee I send this written embassage,

senses.d: To become closely and firmly joined; become compacted.
To grow together.
ex: All those seedlings knitted into a kaleidoscopic border.

senses.d: To combine from various elements.
ex: The witness knitted together his testimony from contradictory pieces of hearsay.

senses.d: To heal following a fracture.
ex: I’ll go skiing again after my bones knit.

senses.d: To form into a knot, or into knots; to tie together, as cord; to fasten by tying.
ex:
When your head did but ache,
I knit my handkercher about your brows,
[He] saw heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending upon him, as it had been a great sheet knit at the four corners […]

senses.d: To draw together; to contract into wrinkles.
A knitted garment.
A session of knitting.
ex: It's always time for a bit of a knit.

grp.label: to make fabric from thread or yarn
to create a stitch by pulling the yarn through from behind

From Middle English knyf, knif, from late Old English cnīf, from Old Norse knífr or Proto-West Germanic *knīb, from Proto-Germanic *knībaz, from *knīpaną (“to pinch”), Proto-Indo-European *gneybʰ- (compare Lithuanian gnýbti, žnýbti (“to pinch”), gnaibis (“pinching”)). Displaced native Middle English sax (“knife”), from Old English seax; and Middle English coutel, qwetyll (“knife”) from Old French coutel. * The verb is first attested in 1865. The variant knive is first attested in 1733.

senses.d: A utensil or a tool designed for cutting, consisting of a flat piece of hard material, usually steel or other metal (the blade), usually sharpened on one edge, attached to a handle. The blade may be pointed for piercing.
ex: He was looking for a knife to chop some steak.
Jeff was bent low over the backboard, working with the knife, a steady sawing motion, his shirt soaked through with sweat.

senses.d: A weapon designed with the aforementioned specifications intended for slashing or stabbing but too short to be called a sword; a dagger.
Any blade-like part in a tool or a machine designed for cutting, such as that of a chipper.
To cut with a knife.
To use a knife to injure or kill by stabbing, slashing, or otherwise using the sharp edge of the knife as a weapon.
ex: She was repeatedly knifed in the chest.
The plane has been hijacked. They've already knifed a guy.

senses.d: To cut through as if with a knife.
ex: The boat knifed through the water.

senses.d: To betray, especially in the context of a political slate.
To positively ignore, especially in order to denigrate; compare cut.
